title: 2 Easy Ways To Build Rapport With Your Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin defines rapport as a connection rooted in students' positive feelings for a teacher, and clarifies that it can't be forced through direct, awkward questioning. Instead, he offers two specific, immediately usable techniques: 'smile until they smile,' used while taking attendance or handing back work, holding eye contact and a smile (or exaggerated expression) until each student reciprocates; and telling a personal childhood story, which he argues is uniquely powerful for making a teacher relatable and building emotional connection. He closes by noting that rapport-building is as much about what a teacher doesn't do — reacting emotionally to misbehavior — as what they actively do, and that the topic will have lasting impact across nearly every area of teaching.
points: Rapport is defined as a connection based on students' positive feelings for the teacher, not something that can be forced through direct questioning.
The 'smile until they smile' technique — used during attendance or passing back work — creates instant, low-effort personal connection with each student.
This technique reportedly works even with older students, including sixth graders, despite assumptions that they are 'too cool' for it.
Telling a personal childhood story is presented as a uniquely powerful rapport-building tool, provided it involves adventure or comedic mishap rather than something overly sensitive.
Building rapport is framed as partly about restraint — avoiding emotional reactions to misbehavior that erect walls between teacher and student.
quotes: Rapport is nothing more than a connection you make with your students based on their positive feelings for you.

To build genuine rapport, you have to draw students to you. You have to use your personality, your humor, and your charisma to get students to want to be around you and take an interest in who you are.
What it does is allow you to make an instant positive and personal connection with each student. It communicates a thousand wonderful things in just a couple of seconds.
Telling a story about your childhood is a good place to start. It places you in an environment they’re unfamiliar picturing you in, but one in which they can closely identify with.

Many teachers have a hard time building rapport because they respond emotionally to misbehavior. They show frustration, they scold, they lecture, and in so doing they erect a giant wall between themselves and their students.
